title: Complex numbers I: algebra and geometry

problems.html: Simplify the powers of the imaginary unit i3,i4,i15,i2026,i−1,i−7.\mathrm{i}^{3},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{4},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{15},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{2026},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{-1},\qquad\allowbreak \mathrm{i}^{-7}.i3,i4,i15,i2026,i−1,i−7.
hints: The powers of i\mathrm{i}i cycle with period 444: i0=1\mathrm{i}^0=1i0=1, i1=i\mathrm{i}^1=\mathrm{i}i1=i, i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1, i3=−i\mathrm{i}^3=-\mathrm{i}i3=−i, and then it begins again.
For a positive exponent, divide by 444 and keep only the remainder — 15=4⋅3+315=4\cdot3+315=4⋅3+3 sends you to i3\mathrm{i}^3i3.

Negative exponents behave the same way once you know i−1=1i=ii2=−i\mathrm{i}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{i}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{i}^2}=-\mathrm{i}i−1=i1​=i2i​=−i; alternatively add multiples of 444 to the exponent until it turns positive.
problems.format: the six values in order, comma-separated

problems.html: With z=3+2iz=3+2\mathrm{i}z=3+2i and w=1−5iw=1-5\mathrm{i}w=1−5i, find z+wz+wz+w, z−wz-wz−w, zwzwzw and z2z^2z2.
hints: Addition and subtraction act part by part: real with real, imaginary with imaginary.
Multiplication is ordinary bracket expansion — the one new rule is that i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 becomes −1-1−1.
Watch the sign as the i2\mathrm{i}^2i2 term joins the real part: in zwzwzw the term −10i2-10\mathrm{i}^2−10i2 contributes +10+10+10, not −10-10−10.
problems.format: z+w, z−w, zw, z² — comma-separated

problems.html: For z=12−5iz=12-5\mathrm{i}z=12−5i find: (a) Rez\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}zRez and Imz\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}zImz;  (b) z‾\overline{z}z;  (c) ∣z∣\left|z\right|∣z∣ and z z‾z\,\overline{z}zz;  (d) Im(iz)\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}(\mathrm{i}z)Im(iz).
hints: Re⁡\operatorname{Re}Re and Im⁡\operatorname{Im}Im both return real numbers: the imaginary part is the coefficient of i\mathrm{i}i, sign included, not a multiple of i\mathrm{i}i.
The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part only. For the modulus, ∣z∣=a2+b2|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}∣z∣=a2+b2​, and the squaring makes the sign of bbb irrelevant.
zzˉz\bar zzzˉ always equals ∣z∣2|z|^2∣z∣2, so use it as a check on your modulus. For (d), multiply out iz\mathrm{i}ziz and put it back into the form a+bia+b\mathrm{i}a+bi before reading anything off.
problems.format: Re z, Im z, z̄, |z|, z·z̄, Im(iz) — commas

problems.html: Write 4+3i1+2i\dfrac{4+3\mathrm{i}}{1+2\mathrm{i}}1+2i4+3i​ in Cartesian form a+b ia+b\,\mathrm{i}a+bi.
hints: To divide, clear the i\mathrm{i}i out of the denominator: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
The denominator then becomes ∣1+2i∣2=12+22|1+2\mathrm{i}|^2=1^2+2^2∣1+2i∣2=12+22, which is real.
Expand the numerator (4+3i)(1−2i)(4+3\mathrm{i})(1-2\mathrm{i})(4+3i)(1−2i) carefully, then divide both of its parts by that real number.
problems.format: Cartesian form a+bi

problems.html: Solve x2+1=0x^2+1=0x2+1=0 and x2+25=0x^2+25=0x2+25=0 over C\mathbb{C}C.
hints: Isolate x2x^2x2 first — each equation says that x2x^2x2 equals a negative real number.
x2=−1x^2=-1x2=−1 has the two solutions ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i: a non-zero number has two square roots.
For the second, look for a real multiple of i\mathrm{i}i: since (ki)2=−k2(k\mathrm{i})^2=-k^2(ki)2=−k2, you need k2=25k^2=25k2=25.
problems.format: the two roots with positive imaginary part

problems.html: On a single Argand diagram, plot the points z1=3+iz_1=3+\mathrm{i}z1​=3+i, z2=−2+2iz_2=-2+2\mathrm{i}z2​=−2+2i and z3=−1−3iz_3=-1-3\mathrm{i}z3​=−1−3i, together with the sum z1+z2z_1+z_2z1​+z2​. Label each point.
hints: Treat a+bia+b\mathrm{i}a+bi as the point (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) and plot exactly as you would in ordinary coordinates.
Addition is vector addition: add the real parts, and separately add the imaginary parts.
Draw the sum tip-to-tail. The four points 000, z1z_1z1​, z1+z2z_1+z_2z1​+z2​ and z2z_2z2​ form a parallelogram — that is the picture worth carrying away.
problems.format: the sum z₁+z₂, as a+bi

problems.html: Convert to polar form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)r(\cos\theta+\mathrm{i}\sin\theta)r(cosθ+isinθ) with principal argument: (a) 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i;  (b) 2i2\mathrm{i}2i;  (c) −3-3−3.  (d) Convert z=2(cos⁡π3+isin⁡π3)z=2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}\bigr)z=2(cos3π​+isin3π​) to Cartesian form.
hints: Polar form needs two numbers: the modulus r=∣z∣r=|z|r=∣z∣, and an angle measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis.
Plot each point before computing anything. The quadrant is what fixes the argument; two of (a)–(c) lie on an axis, where the angle can be read straight off with no arctangent at all.
(d) is the easy direction: substitute the values of cos⁡π3\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}cos3π​ and sin⁡π3\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}sin3π​, then multiply both by the modulus 222.
problems.format: Arg of (a), (b), (c), then Re z in (d); π as pi

problems.html: Let z=3(cos⁡π4+isin⁡π4)z=3\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}\bigr)z=3(cos4π​+isin4π​) and w=2(cos⁡π12+isin⁡π12)w=2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{12}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{12}\bigr)w=2(cos12π​+isin12π​). Using the polar rules, find zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in Cartesian form.
hints: Do not convert to Cartesian form first. In polar form, multiplying multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments.
So zwzwzw has modulus 3⋅23\cdot23⋅2 and argument π4+π12\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\tfrac{\pi}{12}4π​+12π​ — put both fractions over 121212 before adding them.
For z/wz/wz/w, divide the moduli and subtract the arguments. Only once you have the polar answer should you substitute cosine and sine values.
problems.format: modulus and argument of zw; π as pi

problems.html:
Let z=2+3iz=2+3\mathrm{i}z=2+3i and w=1−4iw=1-4\mathrm{i}w=1−4i (as in the notes).

  1. Compute zwzwzw and z/wz/wz/w in Cartesian form.

  2. Verify the conjugate rule zw‾=z‾ w‾\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}zw=zw.

  3. Verify the modulus rule ∣zw∣=∣z∣ ∣w∣\left|zw\right|=\left|z\right|\,\left|w\right|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣.
hints: Part (a) is one expansion and one division; parts (b) and (c) are checks, so compute each side separately and compare.
For z/wz/wz/w, multiply top and bottom by wˉ=1+4i\bar w=1+4\mathrm{i}wˉ=1+4i; the denominator becomes 12+42=171^2+4^2=1712+42=17.
In (c) do not expand anything: ∣z∣=13|z|=\sqrt{13}∣z∣=13​ and ∣w∣=17|w|=\sqrt{17}∣w∣=17​, so the claim is simply that ∣zw∣=13⋅17|zw|=\sqrt{13\cdot17}∣zw∣=13⋅17​.
problems.format: zw in Cartesian form a+bi

problems.html:
(Maths stream — general proofs.) Let z=a+b iz=a+b\,\mathrm{i}z=a+bi and w=c+d iw=c+d\,\mathrm{i}w=c+di with a,b,c,d∈Ra,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}a,b,c,d∈R.

  1. Prove the conjugate-of-a-product rule zw‾=z‾ w‾\overline{zw}=\overline{z}\,\overline{w}zw=zw directly from the definition a+bi‾=a−bi\overline{a+b\mathrm{i}}=a-b\mathrm{i}a+bi​=a−bi.

  2. Using (a) and ∣u∣2=u u‾\left|u\right|^2=u\,\overline{u}∣u∣2=uu, prove that ∣zw∣=∣z∣ ∣w∣\left|zw\right|=\left|z\right|\,\left|w\right|∣zw∣=∣z∣∣w∣.
hints: (a) needs nothing but expansion in a,b,c,da,b,c,da,b,c,d: multiply out zwzwzw, collect it as (real part) +++ (real part) i\,\mathrm{i}i, then conjugate by flipping the sign of that imaginary part.
Now expand zˉ wˉ=(a−bi)(c−di)\bar z\,\bar w=(a-b\mathrm{i})(c-d\mathrm{i})zˉwˉ=(a−bi)(c−di) independently and compare the two results part by part.

For (b), start from ∣zw∣2=(zw) zw‾|zw|^2=(zw)\,\overline{zw}∣zw∣2=(zw)zw; part (a) lets you rewrite the conjugate, and the four factors then regroup into two pairs. Why is it enough to show that the squares agree?
problems.format: conj(zw), then |zw|², for z=1+2i, w=3−i

problems.html: Solve over C\mathbb{C}C, and confirm that the roots form a conjugate pair: (a) x2+2x+10=0x^2+2x+10=0x2+2x+10=0, by completing the square; (b) 2x2+x+1=02x^2+x+1=02x2+x+1=0, by the quadratic formula.
hints: The method is unchanged from real quadratics; the only difference is that a negative number under the square root is now allowed rather than fatal.

In (a), rewrite x2+2xx^2+2xx2+2x as a perfect square minus a constant, so the equation says (perfect square) === a negative number. A negative number −q-q−q has the two square roots ±iq\pm\mathrm{i}\sqrt q±iq​.

In (b), identify aaa, bbb, ccc first; the discriminant is negative, so write b2−4ac\sqrt{b^2-4ac}b2−4ac​ as i4ac−b2\mathrm{i}\sqrt{4ac-b^2}i4ac−b2​. Check that the two roots multiply back to a real quadratic factor.
problems.format: (a) root with Im>0, then Re of (b)'s roots (decimal)

problems.html:
1. Let z=3+2iz=3+2\mathrm{i}z=3+2i and w=−1+2iw=-1+2\mathrm{i}w=−1+2i. Plot z, w, z‾, z+w, z−wz,\ w,\ \overline{z},\ z+w,\ z-wz, w, z, z+w, z−w on an Argand diagram, and compute the distance ∣z−w∣\left|z-w\right|∣z−w∣ between the points zzz and www.

  2. (Data science — distance between records.) Two data points in the plane are encoded as p=2+5ip=2+5\mathrm{i}p=2+5i and q=6+2iq=6+2\mathrm{i}q=6+2i. Compute the Euclidean distance ∣p−q∣\left|p-q\right|∣p−q∣ between them and the midpoint 12(p+q)\tfrac12(p+q)21​(p+q).
hints: Plot each number as the point (a,b)(a,b)(a,b): the conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis, and z+wz+wz+w comes from the parallelogram rule.
∣z−w∣|z-w|∣z−w∣ is the distance between the two points: subtract part by part first, then take the modulus. In (a) the two points share an imaginary part — what does that make z−wz-wz−w?
In (b) the same distance reading applies to the two records. The midpoint is the average 12(p+q)\tfrac12(p+q)21​(p+q): average the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.
problems.format: z+w, z−w, z̄, |z−w|, |p−q|, midpoint; decimals

problems.html: Convert each number to polar form, giving the principal argument Argz∈(−π,π]\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}z\in(-\pi,\pi]Argz∈(−π,π]. Sketch each to fix the quadrant. (a) 1+i;(b) −1+i;(c) −2−23 i;(d) 3−i;(e) −5.\text{(a)}\ 1+\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ -1+\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ -2-2\sqrt3\,\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ \sqrt3-\mathrm{i};\qquad\allowbreak \text{(e)}\ -5.(a) 1+i;(b) −1+i;(c) −2−23​i;(d) 3​−i;(e) −5.
hints: Sketch each point first. The modulus is never in doubt; it is the argument that goes wrong when a calculator is trusted blindly.
Get the reference angle from arctan⁡∣b/a∣\arctan|b/a|arctan∣b/a∣, then place it in the correct quadrant and adjust until it lies inside (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π].
A third-quadrant point has a negative principal argument, and a point on the negative real axis has argument exactly π\piπ — not −π-\pi−π, which the interval excludes.
problems.format: the five principal arguments; π as pi

problems.html:
(Physics — AC circuits.) A series circuit has complex impedance Z=4+3iZ=4+3\mathrm{i}Z=4+3i (in ohms). It is driven by a voltage V=10V=10V=10 (volts, taken as a real reference).

  1. Find ∣Z∣\left|Z\right|∣Z∣ and the phase angle ArgZ\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}ZArgZ.

  2. Compute the current I=V/ZI=V/ZI=V/Z in Cartesian form and its magnitude ∣I∣\left|I\right|∣I∣.
hints: The modulus and phase angle of ZZZ are just its polar form; sketch 4+3i4+3\mathrm{i}4+3i to confirm the quadrant before trusting an arctangent.
4+3i4+3\mathrm{i}4+3i is a 333–444–555 triangle, so the modulus is a whole number. It lies in the first quadrant, so arctan⁡(3/4)\arctan(3/4)arctan(3/4) is the correct principal argument here.
For the current, divide by multiplying top and bottom by Zˉ=4−3i\bar Z=4-3\mathrm{i}Zˉ=4−3i. Then check with ∣I∣=∣V∣/∣Z∣|I|=|V|/|Z|∣I∣=∣V∣/∣Z∣, which sidesteps the arithmetic entirely.
problems.format: |Z|, then I as a+bi, then |I|

problems.html: Let z=2(cos⁡3π4+isin⁡3π4)z=\sqrt2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{3\pi}{4}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\bigr)z=2​(cos43π​+isin43π​) and w=2(cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2)w=2\bigl(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\bigr)w=2(cos2π​+isin2π​). Find (a) zwzwzw and (b) z/wz/wz/w, giving each in polar form with the principal argument and in Cartesian form.
hints: Both numbers are already in polar form, so use the polar rules and convert to Cartesian form only at the very end.
For zwzwzw multiply the moduli and add the arguments; for z/wz/wz/w divide the moduli and subtract them.
Is 3π4+π2\tfrac{3\pi}{4}+\tfrac{\pi}{2}43π​+2π​ inside (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π]? If not, add or subtract one whole turn 2π2\pi2π before calling it the principal argument.
problems.format: Arg(zw), zw, then z/w — a+bi, decimals, π as pi

problems.html:
1. For z=2+iz=2+\mathrm{i}z=2+i, compute iz\mathrm{i}ziz and confirm geometrically that multiplying by i\mathrm{i}i is a quarter-turn anticlockwise that preserves length.

  2. Which single complex number rotates a point by π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​ anticlockwise and doubles its distance from the origin?

  3. Apply a clockwise quarter-turn to 3+i3+\mathrm{i}3+i (i.e. multiply by the number of modulus 111 and argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​).

  4. (Physics — phasors.) A voltage phasor V1=6+8iV_1=6+8\mathrm{i}V1​=6+8i is joined by a second phasor V2V_2V2​ of equal amplitude turned a quarter-turn anticlockwise, i.e. V2=iV1V_2=\mathrm{i}V_1V2​=iV1​. Find V2V_2V2​, the resultant V=V1+V2V=V_1+V_2V=V1​+V2​ in Cartesian form, and its amplitude ∣V∣\left|V\right|∣V∣.
hints: Multiplying by a number of modulus 111 rotates without changing length, and i\mathrm{i}i has modulus 111 and argument π2\tfrac{\pi}{2}2π​. Test the claim in (a) by comparing ∣z∣|z|∣z∣ with ∣iz∣|\mathrm{i}z|∣iz∣.
(b) needs a rotation and a stretch at once: what modulus and argument must the multiplier have? For (c), which number has modulus 111 and argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​?
(d): V2=iV1V_2=\mathrm{i}V_1V2​=iV1​ needs no trigonometry — expand it, then add the two phasors part by part. Two equal phasors at right angles also give a quick check on ∣V∣|V|∣V∣.
problems.format: (a), (b), (c), then V in (d) — a+bi, commas

problems.html:
(Conceptual — true or false, with a one-line reason.)

  1. For every z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C, z2≥0z^2\ge0z2≥0.

  2. ∣z∣=∣z‾∣\left|z\right|=\left|\overline{z}\right|∣z∣=∣z∣ for all zzz.

  3. If z+z‾=0z+\overline{z}=0z+z=0 then zzz is purely imaginary or zero.

  4. Re(zw)=Re(z) Re(w)\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(zw)=\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(z)\,\mathop{\mathrm{Re}}(w)Re(zw)=Re(z)Re(w) for all z,wz,wz,w.

  5. There is an ordering <<< on C\mathbb{C}C compatible with its arithmetic — that is, one respecting +++ and ×\times× (if x>0x>0x>0 and y>0y>0y>0 then x+y>0x+y>0x+y>0 and xy>0xy>0xy>0), so that every nonzero square is positive.
hints: Each is settled by a one-line reason or a single counterexample. Try z=iz=\mathrm{i}z=i first — it breaks several plausible-looking claims.
For (a), ask whether '≥0\ge 0≥0' even means anything for a number that is not real. For (c), what is z+zˉz+\bar zz+zˉ in terms of Re⁡z\operatorname{Re}zRez?
For (e), suppose such an ordering existed. Every non-zero square would have to be positive; apply that to 1=121=1^21=12 and to −1=i2-1=\mathrm{i}^2−1=i2 and see what you are forced to conclude.
problems.format: (a)–(e): true or false, comma-separated

problems.html: (Rotation/geometry.) Two vertices of an equilateral triangle lie at 000 and 222 on the real axis. Use multiplication by a complex number of modulus 111 to find the two possible positions of the third vertex.
hints: The third vertex comes from a known side by rotating it about a vertex, and a rotation is multiplication by a number of modulus 111.
Rotating the number 222 about the origin through π3\tfrac{\pi}{3}3π​ means multiplying it by cos⁡π3+isin⁡π3\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}cos3π​+isin3π​.
Both signs of the angle give a genuine triangle, one above the real axis and one below. Check each candidate is at distance 222 from both 000 and 222.
problems.format: the third vertex's real part, then its modulus

problems.html: Find the real numbers x,yx,yx,y satisfying (x+y i)(3−i)=7+i(x+y\,\mathrm{i})(3-\mathrm{i})=7+\mathrm{i}(x+yi)(3−i)=7+i.
hints: Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree — that turns one complex equation into two real ones.
Expand (x+yi)(3−i)(x+y\mathrm{i})(3-\mathrm{i})(x+yi)(3−i) and collect it into that shape; you should reach (3x+y)+(3y−x)i(3x+y)+(3y-x)\mathrm{i}(3x+y)+(3y−x)i.
Now solve the simultaneous pair 3x+y=73x+y=73x+y=7 and 3y−x=13y-x=13y−x=1, then substitute back into the original product as a check.
problems.format: x, y — comma-separated

problems.html: Simplify to Cartesian form: (a) 1+2i3−4i\dfrac{1+2\mathrm{i}}{3-4\mathrm{i}}3−4i1+2i​; (b) i1+i\dfrac{\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}1+ii​.
hints: Both are divisions, so both begin the same way: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
In (a) the denominator becomes 32+42=253^2+4^2=2532+42=25.
In (b) the numerator is just i(1−i)=i−i2\mathrm{i}(1-\mathrm{i})=\mathrm{i}-\mathrm{i}^2i(1−i)=i−i2, and that −i2-\mathrm{i}^2−i2 contributes a real +1+1+1.
problems.format: (a), (b) as a+bi, decimals

problems.html: Given that 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i is a root of x3−4x2+9x−10=0x^3-4x^2+9x-10=0x3−4x2+9x−10=0 (real coefficients), find the other two roots.
hints: The coefficients are real, and that fact alone hands you a second root for nothing.

Complex roots of a real polynomial come in conjugate pairs. The pair α,αˉ\alpha,\bar\alphaα,αˉ gives the real quadratic factor (x−α)(x−αˉ)=x2−2Re⁡(α) x+∣α∣2(x-\alpha)(x-\bar\alpha)=x^2-2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha)\,x+|\alpha|^2(x−α)(x−αˉ)=x2−2Re(α)x+∣α∣2.
What is left is a linear factor x−kx-kx−k. Compare the constant terms of the cubic and of (quadratic)×(x−k)\times(x-k)×(x−k) to find kkk, then expand the product as a check.
problems.format: the other two roots, comma-separated

problems.html: Describe geometrically, and sketch, the set of points z∈Cz\in\mathbb{C}z∈C satisfying (a) ∣z∣=2;(b) ∣z−1∣=3;(c) ∣z−i∣=∣z+i∣;(d) ∣z−1∣<2.\text{(a)}\ \left|z\right|=2;\qquad\allowbreak \text{(b)}\ \left|z-1\right|=3;\qquad\allowbreak \text{(c)}\ \left|z-\mathrm{i}\right|=\left|z+\mathrm{i}\right|;\qquad\allowbreak \text{(d)}\ \left|z-1\right|<2.(a) ∣z∣=2;(b) ∣z−1∣=3;(c) ∣z−i∣=∣z+i∣;(d) ∣z−1∣<2. For (d), shade the region and show clearly whether its boundary is included.
hints: Read every modulus as a distance: ∣z−c∣|z-c|∣z−c∣ is the distance from the point zzz to the point ccc.
So (a) and (b) each say 'stay at a fixed distance from a fixed point' — read the centre and the radius straight off. (d) is the inequality version of the same kind of condition.

In (c) the condition is 'equally far from i\mathrm{i}i and from −i-\mathrm{i}−i'; confirm your answer by putting z=x+yiz=x+y\mathrm{i}z=x+yi. In (d) draw the boundary first, dashed because the inequality is strict, then shade the side that satisfies it.
problems.format: (a)–(d): circle, line or disc, commas

problems.html: Compute the product (1+i)(3+i)(1+\mathrm{i})(\sqrt3+\mathrm{i})(1+i)(3​+i) in two ways — by Cartesian expansion and by the polar rule — and hence write down its modulus and argument.
hints: The point of the exercise is that the two routes must agree, so carry them out independently and only then compare.
For the polar route you need each factor in polar form: 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i has modulus 2\sqrt22​ and argument π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​; find the same two numbers for 3+i\sqrt3+\mathrm{i}3​+i.
The product's modulus is the product of the moduli and its argument the sum of the arguments. Matching the two forms afterwards even hands you the exact cosine and sine of that awkward angle.
problems.format: the argument of the product; π as pi

problems.html: Suppose ∣z∣=2\left|z\right|=2∣z∣=2, Argz=π3\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}z=\tfrac{\pi}{3}Argz=3π​, ∣w∣=3\left|w\right|=3∣w∣=3, Argw=π4\mathop{\mathrm{Arg}}w=\tfrac{\pi}{4}Argw=4π​. Find the modulus and argument of (a) zwzwzw, (b) z/wz/wz/w, (c) z2z^2z2 and (d) z‾\overline{z}z; (e) convert zzz and z2z^2z2 to Cartesian form.
hints: Nothing here needs Cartesian form until the very last part — work with moduli and arguments throughout.
Multiply moduli and add arguments; divide moduli and subtract arguments; and for z2z^2z2 square the modulus while doubling the argument.
Conjugating leaves the modulus alone and negates the argument. Convert zzz and z2z^2z2 at the end, then check by squaring your Cartesian zzz directly.

problems.html: Prove the parallelogram law: for all z,w∈Cz,w\in\mathbb{C}z,w∈C, ∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2∣z∣2+2∣w∣2.\left|z+w\right|^2+\left|z-w\right|^2=2\left|z\right|^2+2\left|w\right|^2.∣z+w∣2+∣z−w∣2=2∣z∣2+2∣w∣2.
hints: Do not break into xxx and yyy. Use ∣ζ∣2=ζζˉ|\zeta|^2=\zeta\bar\zeta∣ζ∣2=ζζˉ​ throughout and the whole proof is two expansions.
Expand ∣z+w∣2=(z+w)(zˉ+wˉ)|z+w|^2=(z+w)(\bar z+\bar w)∣z+w∣2=(z+w)(zˉ+wˉ) and ∣z−w∣2=(z−w)(zˉ−wˉ)|z-w|^2=(z-w)(\bar z-\bar w)∣z−w∣2=(z−w)(zˉ−wˉ) separately.
Now add the two lines and look at the cross terms zwˉz\bar wzwˉ and zˉw\bar z wzˉw: they appear with opposite signs, which is the whole trick.

problems.html: Find all z=x+y iz=x+y\,\mathrm{i}z=x+yi (with x,y∈Rx,y\in\mathbb{R}x,y∈R) such that z2=3+4iz^2=3+4\mathrm{i}z2=3+4i, working directly in Cartesian form.
hints: Write z=x+yiz=x+y\mathrm{i}z=x+yi, square it, and match real and imaginary parts against 3+4i3+4\mathrm{i}3+4i.
That gives the pair x2−y2=3x^2-y^2=3x2−y2=3 and 2xy=42xy=42xy=4; use the second to eliminate yyy.

Substituting y=2/xy=2/xy=2/x produces x4−3x2−4=0x^4-3x^2-4=0x4−3x2−4=0, a quadratic in x2x^2x2. Only the non-negative root of that is usable, since xxx is real — and then xy=2>0xy=2>0xy=2>0 fixes the sign of yyy.

questions.stem: Why is i\mathrm{i}i defined by the property i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1 rather than by writing i=−1\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}i=−1​?
options: Because i\mathrm{i}i is not a square root of anything.
The two are equivalent; i2=−1\mathrm{i}^2=-1i2=−1 is simply shorter to write.
Because manipulating −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ with the usual surd rule leads to 1=−11=-11=−1.
Because −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ would have to be a real number.
questions.hint: Apply the surd rule xy=xy\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{xy}x​y​=xy​ to (−1)(−1)\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}(−1)(−1)​ and see what it ends up claiming.
questions.why: The rule xy=xy\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}=\sqrt{xy}x​y​=xy​ holds only for non-negative reals. Applied blindly it gives 1=1=(−1)(−1)=−1 −1=i⋅i=−11=\sqrt{1}=\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}=\sqrt{-1}\,\sqrt{-1}=\mathrm{i}\cdot\mathrm{i}=-11=1​=(−1)(−1)​=−1​−1​=i⋅i=−1, which is a genuine contradiction rather than a curiosity. Defining i\mathrm{i}i by the property it must satisfy means the symbol −1\sqrt{-1}−1​ never has to be manipulated at all. There is a second, quieter reason too: −1-1−1 has two square roots, ±i\pm\mathrm{i}±i, and no principled way to call one of them 'the' square root.

questions.stem: A student simplifies 2+3i1+i\dfrac{2+3\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}1+i2+3i​ to 21+31i=2+3i\dfrac21+\dfrac31\mathrm{i}=2+3\mathrm{i}12​+13​i=2+3i. What has gone wrong?
options: The moduli should have been divided instead of the parts.
Nothing, as long as the denominator is non-zero.
The sign of the imaginary part was dropped; the answer is 2−3i2-3\mathrm{i}2−3i.
Division is not done part by part; multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
questions.hint: Test the student's rule on a case you can check independently: does 1+i1+i\dfrac{1+\mathrm{i}}{1+\mathrm{i}}1+i1+i​ come out as 111 that way?
questions.why: In general a+bic+di≠ac+bdi\dfrac{a+b\mathrm{i}}{c+d\mathrm{i}}\neq\dfrac{a}{c}+\dfrac{b}{d}\mathrm{i}c+dia+bi​=ca​+db​i — addition and subtraction split part by part, but division does not. Multiplying top and bottom by 1−i1-\mathrm{i}1−i makes the denominator real: (2+3i)(1−i)12+12=5+i2=52+12i\dfrac{(2+3\mathrm{i})(1-\mathrm{i})}{1^2+1^2}=\dfrac{5+\mathrm{i}}{2}=\tfrac52+\tfrac12\mathrm{i}12+12(2+3i)(1−i)​=25+i​=25​+21​i, which is nothing like 2+3i2+3\mathrm{i}2+3i. Dividing moduli is a real rule, but it belongs to polar form and gives only the modulus of the answer, not the answer.

questions.stem: Both 1+i1+\mathrm{i}1+i and −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i satisfy tan⁡θ=1\tan\theta=1tanθ=1. What is the principal argument of −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i?
options: −3π4-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}−43π​.
π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}4π​, since arctan⁡1=π4\arctan 1=\tfrac{\pi}{4}arctan1=4π​.
5π4\tfrac{5\pi}{4}45π​.

questions.hint: Sketch the point first. Which quadrant is it in, and which interval must a *principal* argument lie in?

Here −1−i-1-\mathrm{i}−1−i is in the third quadrant, so its argument is π4+π=5π4\tfrac{\pi}{4}+\pi=\tfrac{5\pi}{4}4π​+π=45π​. That is a perfectly correct argument, but the principal one is required to lie in (−π,π](-\pi,\pi](−π,π], so subtract 2π2\pi2π to get −3π4-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}−43π​.

questions.stem: Which single complex number rotates a point a quarter-turn anticlockwise about the origin and doubles its distance from the origin?
options: i2\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}2i​
−2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i
222
2i2\mathrm{i}2i
questions.hint: Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments. Write down the modulus and the argument the answer must have, then find the option with both.
questions.why: Multiplying by www multiplies moduli and adds arguments, so the doubling needs ∣w∣=2|w|=2∣w∣=2 and the anticlockwise quarter-turn needs arg⁡w=π2\arg w=\tfrac{\pi}{2}argw=2π​. That number is 2(cos⁡π2+isin⁡π2)=2i2\left(\cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)=2\mathrm{i}2(cos2π​+isin2π​)=2i. Each wrong option gets exactly one half right: 222 has argument 000, so it scales without turning; −2i-2\mathrm{i}−2i has argument −π2-\tfrac{\pi}{2}−2π​, a clockwise quarter-turn; and i2\tfrac{\mathrm{i}}{2}2i​ turns the right way but halves the distance instead of doubling it.

questions.stem: A student writes ∣3+4i∣=3+4=7|3+4\mathrm{i}|=3+4=7∣3+4i∣=3+4=7. What is the modulus, and why?
options: 555, by Pythagoras on the real and imaginary parts.
777 — the modulus is the sum of the two parts.
252525, since ∣z∣2=zzˉ|z|^2=z\bar z∣z∣2=zzˉ.
7\sqrt77​.
questions.hint: The modulus is a distance in the plane, from the origin to (3,4)(3,4)(3,4). Which triangle has legs 333 and 444?
questions.why: The modulus is the distance from the origin to the point (3,4)(3,4)(3,4), so it is 32+42=25=5\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=532+42​=25​=5 — the familiar 333–444–555 triangle. Adding the parts has no geometric meaning and would even give a different answer for 3−4i3-4\mathrm{i}3−4i, whose distance from the origin is plainly the same. The value 252525 is ∣z∣2=zzˉ|z|^2=z\bar z∣z∣2=zzˉ, which is genuinely useful — it is what makes the conjugate trick work for division — but it is the square of the modulus, not the modulus.

questions.stem: A cubic with real coefficients has 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i among its roots. What follows immediately?
options: −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i is also a root.
Nothing — a cubic may have any three roots.
1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i is also a root, and the third root is real.
All three roots are non-real.
questions.hint: Real coefficients force non-real roots to occur in conjugate pairs. Count how many of the three roots that uses up, and what it leaves.
questions.why: Real coefficients force non-real roots to occur in conjugate pairs, so 1−2i1-2\mathrm{i}1−2i is a root as well. That uses up two of the three, and the remaining one must be real, since a third non-real root would need its own conjugate partner and there is no room left. Note that the conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part only: −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i is the negation, not the conjugate, and is not forced to be anything.

questions.stem: In the Argand plane, which set of points satisfies ∣z−(1+2i)∣=3\left|z-(1+2\mathrm{i})\right|=3∣z−(1+2i)∣=3?
options: The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining 000 to 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i.
The circle of radius 333 centred at −1−2i-1-2\mathrm{i}−1−2i.
The disc of radius 333 centred at 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i, its boundary included.
The circle of radius 333 centred at 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i.
questions.hint: Read ∣z−w∣\left|z-w\right|∣z−w∣ as a distance. Between which two points, and what shape is traced by holding a distance fixed?
questions.why: ∣z−w∣\left|z-w\right|∣z−w∣ is the distance between the points zzz and www, so the equation says: stay exactly 333 away from 1+2i1+2\mathrm{i}1+2i. Points at a fixed distance from a centre form a circle, and the centre is the number being subtracted, not its negative — the minus sign is part of the distance, not a reflection. It is worth writing a locus in the form ∣z−w∣\left|z-w\right|∣z−w∣ before reading the centre off: ∣z+3∣\left|z+3\right|∣z+3∣ is ∣z−(−3)∣\left|z-(-3)\right|∣z−(−3)∣ and so is centred at −3-3−3. A disc would need ≤\le≤ in place of ===, and a perpendicular bisector comes from setting two distances equal, as in ∣z∣=∣z−w∣\left|z\right|=\left|z-w\right|∣z∣=∣z−w∣.

questions.stem: Is the statement 2+3i>1+i2+3\mathrm{i}>1+\mathrm{i}2+3i>1+i meaningful?
options: Yes — compare the moduli, and ∣2+3i∣>∣1+i∣\left|2+3\mathrm{i}\right|>\left|1+\mathrm{i}\right|∣2+3i∣>∣1+i∣.
Yes — compare the real parts, and 2>12>12>1.
Only for two numbers lying in the same quadrant.
No: there is no ordering of C\mathbb{C}C compatible with its arithmetic.
questions.hint: Suppose an ordering existed and behaved like the one on R\mathbb{R}R, where a non-zero square is always positive. Try that on i\mathrm{i}i.
questions.why: Any ordering that gets on with the arithmetic the way the real one does would make every non-zero square positive. Applying that to i\mathrm{i}i gives i2=−1>0\mathrm{i}^{2}=-1>0i2=−1>0, which is false, and the same contradiction arrives whichever sign is assigned to i\mathrm{i}i. So C\mathbb{C}C carries no such ordering, and >>> between two complex numbers means nothing. Real parts and moduli are perfectly good things to compare — they are real numbers — but neither orders C\mathbb{C}C: the modulus makes 111 and i\mathrm{i}i tie without being equal, and the real part makes 3i3\mathrm{i}3i and 000 tie. This is a real difference from R\mathbb{R}R, not a gap in the notation.

questions.stem: How many solutions has z2=−9z^{2}=-9z2=−9 in C\mathbb{C}C, and what are they?
options: One, z=3iz=3\mathrm{i}z=3i.
Two, z=±3iz=\pm 3\mathrm{i}z=±3i.
Two, z=±9iz=\pm 9\mathrm{i}z=±9i.
None: a square cannot be negative.
questions.hint: Square each candidate and see. Then ask how many roots a quadratic is entitled to over C\mathbb{C}C.
questions.why: (3i)2=9i2=−9(3\mathrm{i})^{2}=9\mathrm{i}^{2}=-9(3i)2=9i2=−9, and (−3i)2(-3\mathrm{i})^{2}(−3i)2 is the same, so both work: z=±3iz=\pm3\mathrm{i}z=±3i. "A square cannot be negative" is a statement about real numbers, and it has no analogue over C\mathbb{C}C — which is precisely why C\mathbb{C}C cannot be ordered. There are two roots rather than one because a degree-222 polynomial has two roots counted with multiplicity, and here they are distinct. Checking the size catches ±9i\pm9\mathrm{i}±9i: its square is −81-81−81.
